slides.say: Nagarjuna's Fundamental Verses on the Middle Way. Chapter twenty-three: the examination of errors.

slides.heading: Where do greed and anger come from?
points: Praise warms; an insult hardens
Beauty seems to be in the face, the insult in the words
Are these qualities found where we feel them?
slides.say: Someone praises you, and something warms. Someone insults you, and something hardens. A face looks beautiful, a smell disgusting, a loss unbearable. These reactions feel like responses to what is simply there: the beauty in the face, the insult in the words. Chapter twenty-three asks where greed, anger and confusion really come from, and whether the qualities that seem to set them off are found where we feel them to be.

slides.heading: The shape of the chapter
points: The afflictions: what practice sets out to remove
If they had their own nature, nothing could remove them
If they were nothing, there would be nothing to remove
A third way: they end when their mistakes are seen through
slides.say: The chapter is about the afflictions, the states that Buddhist practice sets out to remove. It follows directly from the examination of the self in chapter eighteen and of bondage and liberation in chapter sixteen. If the afflictions had a nature of their own, nothing could remove them. If they were simply nothing, there would be nothing to remove. Nagarjuna shows a third way to see them: they arise from mistaken ways of taking things, and they end when those mistakes are seen through.

slides.heading: The verses
points: A new translation from the Sanskrit
The Sanskrit is shown above each verse
slides.say: First, the verses. The translation is new, made from the Sanskrit for this site.

slides.heading: Where the afflictions come from
slides.say: Now the explanation. The chapter opens with a teaching every Buddhist school accepts. Desire, hatred and delusion spring from conceptual thinking. More exactly, they come about in dependence on three supports. Desire depends on what seems attractive. Hatred depends on what seems unattractive. Delusion depends on the inversions, the four mistaken ways of taking things. This is how Chandrakirti reads the verse. We do not first meet a beautiful thing and then, as a separate matter, want it. The wanting rides on a way of taking the thing: as beautiful from its own side, in a way that seems to call for possession. Nagarjuna draws the consequence at once. Whatever arises in dependence on such supports does not have a nature of its own. The afflictions are real enough as experiences. Anger burns, craving pulls. But they are not solid lumps in the mind with fixed natures. They are what a certain way of seeing produces, and they can end when the mistake is seen through.

slides.heading: Whose afflictions?
points: Afflictions are always someone's
The owner is not found from its own side
Anger and the angry one: designated together
slides.say: Verses three to five bring back the result of the chapter on the self. Afflictions are always someone's: my anger, your craving. But the self has been sought and not found as existing from its own side, and not found as simply non-existent either. If the owner is not established, the afflictions cannot be established as the owner's possessions. Verse five uses the fivefold analysis. The anger is not the same as the angry person, not separate from them, not inside them, not containing them, not owned by them as a separate thing. Each is designated in relation to the other. Neither is found standing alone.

slides.heading: Like a mirage
points: The six kinds of sense object carry beauty or ugliness
Go to a mirage for water: none is found
Go into the object for the beauty: it is not found
slides.say: The heart of the chapter is verses six to twelve. If the afflictions depend on the attractive, the unattractive and the inversions, are those supports any firmer? They are not: none of them exists by its own nature. The objects that seem to carry these qualities are the six kinds of sense object: forms, sounds, tastes, touches, smells and mental objects. But taken on their own, without the mind's addition, these objects are like a mirage or a dream. A mirage shows water. Go to it for a drink and no water is found. In the same way, the object shows beauty or ugliness. Go into the object for the beauty and it is not found.

slides.heading: Attractive and unattractive, named together
slides.say: Then the decisive step. Unattractive can only be named by reference to attractive, and attractive only by reference to unattractive. Each is defined against the other, like tall and short, near and far. Neither is a quality sitting in a thing on its own. The same meal is delicious to the hungry and sickening to the overfed; the same song is beautiful at a wedding and painful at a funeral. So, if the attractive is not found on its own, where does desire get its grip? If the unattractive is not found on its own, where does hatred get its grip? This is not a recipe for feeling nothing. Food still tastes good and a cut still hurts. What loosens is the sense that the goodness or badness is lodged in the thing, demanding that we seize it or destroy it.

slides.heading: The four mistakes, and their opposites
slides.say: Buddhist teaching names four inversions: taking what is impermanent as permanent, what is suffering as pleasant, what is not-self as self, and what is impure as pure. The path corrects them by seeing impermanence, suffering, not-self and impurity. Nagarjuna accepts the teaching and pushes it one step further. In what is empty, no impermanent thing is found any more than a permanent one. If permanent is a wrong grasp, then impermanent, grasped as the real nature of a real thing, is also a grasp. The correction can become a new fixation. The instrument of grasping, the act, the one who grasps and the thing grasped are all at peace; none is found on its own. And, as in chapter two, mistakes are not found to arise for someone already mistaken, nor for someone not mistaken, nor for someone in the middle of being mistaken. So the opposites are true as correctives. Like medicine, they do their work and are not kept once the illness has gone.

slides.heading: How the afflictions end
slides.say: When the mistakes cease, ignorance ceases, and with it the whole chain of the twelve links. Here is the practical point of the chapter. Afflictions are not removed by force, like stones lifted out of a field. They end when the mistake that feeds them is seen through. The last two verses close the alternatives. If afflictions were real by their own nature, they could not be abandoned, because a nature that is really a thing's own cannot be taken away from it. If lacking own-nature meant that they simply do not exist, they could not be abandoned either, because there would be nothing to abandon. Practice needs afflictions that are real enough to hurt and empty enough to end. Only because they arise in dependence on mistaken views can they cease when the views cease.

slides.heading: What is left standing
points: Desire and anger still arise and still hurt
Fresh bread is still told from mould
The four inversions remain a true diagnosis
slides.say: Desire, anger and confusion are not explained away. They arise, they hurt, and they shape lives. The attractive and the unattractive are still told apart: fresh bread from mould, a kind word from a cruel one. Ethics and practice keep their full force, and the four inversions keep their place as a true diagnosis. What goes is the idea that these qualities sit in things, and that the afflictions are solid states owned by a solid self.

slides.heading: Check it now
points: Notice the next flash of irritation
Look for the irritating quality in the sound or the words
Not found there; yet it was felt, and can relax
slides.say: Notice the next flash of irritation. Look for the irritating quality in the sound, the person or the words, apart from your taking of them. It is not found there. Yet the irritation was felt, and it can now relax without being suppressed. That is the whole method of the chapter, in one moment.

slides.heading: In the books
points: Substrateless World: Introduction and Chapter 1
The Logic of Dependency: two sections
Innate grasping, and anger changed by its conditions
slides.say: The two books take up these themes in several places. In The Logical Necessity of a Substrateless World, the Introduction, in Why It Matters, locates suffering not in appearances but in reading them as more than they are; and chapter one describes the innate grasping that the afflictions ride on. The bonus article, The Logic of Dependency, gives Tsongkhapa's advice to look for the object of negation when falsely accused or unexpectedly praised, and shows anger changed by changing its conditions rather than removed like a stone. Links to all of them are on the chapter page. Next: chapter twenty-four, the examination of the four noble truths.
